_what: Things that are suspected but not proved, ordered from the widest reach to the most local. Each is told as a short account for someone new to the subject: what has been found so far, and what is probably happening beyond it. None of it is evidence, and none of it is counted in the map's figures.

items.title: Oil and gas producers inside the UN climate talks
items.claim: People working for oil and gas producers are probably helping to negotiate the wording of UN climate agreements from inside government delegations and summit presidencies, not only lobbying from outside.
items.rule: A national oil company's chief executive presided over COP28; thousands of fossil fuel lobbyists attend each summit, many on national delegations; the talks decide by consensus, so one delegation can strike a sentence.
items.conditions: Delegations are chosen by governments with no limit on who joins them; affiliations were not recorded before 2024; negotiating rooms are closed.
items.documented: Kick Big Polluters Out counts for COP26 to COP30; the COP28 presidency.
items.would_show: Negotiating records or testimony showing a company employee on a national delegation drafting or blocking agreed text on the company's instruction.
items.would_refute: Delegation records showing no industry staff in negotiating rooms and no text changes traced to them.
story: The UN climate summit held in Dubai at the end of 2023, COP28, was presided over by the chief executive of the United Arab Emirates' national oil company. During the summit he said that phasing out fossil fuels would take the world back into caves.

Every year a coalition of more than 450 organisations, Kick Big Polluters Out, goes through the official list of participants line by line. It counted at least 2,456 fossil fuel lobbyists in Dubai, 1,773 at the next summit in Baku, and more than 1,600 at Belém in Brazil in 2025, where about one person in every 25 worked for the industry. In Baku they outnumbered every national delegation except three. Many did not come as observers but as members of government delegations. European Union countries alone brought more than 113 to Baku. The 90 companies that sent lobbyists between 2021 and 2024 produced 57 per cent of the world's oil and gas in 2024.
Until 2024 the UN climate body did not record who participants worked for. The final agreement at Belém did not mention fossil fuels.

These talks decide by consensus, so one delegation can remove a sentence from the text. The wording of the agreements is probably negotiated in part by people who work for oil and gas producers, sitting on government delegations and running summit presidencies, as well as by lobbyists in the corridors.

items.title: The largest money managers running central banks' rescue operations
items.claim: A few of the world's largest asset managers have probably become part of central banks' and finance ministries' crisis machinery in several countries, spending public money in markets where they hold large positions of their own.
items.rule: The Federal Reserve hired BlackRock without tender in 2020 to run its bond purchases, and nearly half of its ETF purchases went into BlackRock's own funds; the European Union hired the same firm to advise on bank risk rules the same spring.
items.conditions: In a crisis central banks need traders at once and few firms have them; contracts can be awarded without tender; the same firms own large parts of the markets being supported.
items.documented: Federal Reserve disclosures of May 2020; reporting by Bloomberg, Reuters and the Globe and Mail.
items.would_show: Evidence that an asset manager running a public programme shaped its terms or purchases to benefit its own holdings.
items.would_refute: Audits of the 2020 programmes and similar contracts elsewhere finding purchases matched market weights and no influence on programme design.
story: On 23 March 2020, as markets fell, the US Federal Reserve announced it would buy corporate bonds and, for the first time in its history, exchange-traded funds, which are bundles of bonds or shares that trade like a single share. The next day the New York Fed hired BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, to do the buying. There was no competitive tender. The programmes could have grown to 750 billion dollars.

BlackRock is also the largest seller of exchange-traded funds. When the Fed published its first purchases in May, 48 per cent of the money it had spent on these funds had gone into BlackRock's own iShares funds. BlackRock waived its fees on them, and the Fed chair told the Senate the firm was chosen for its expertise and because the Fed had to move fast. Emails released later showed that he spoke to BlackRock's chief executive on 23 March, hours after the programme was announced. A month later the European Union hired BlackRock to advise on how European banks should take environmental and social risks into account.

In a crisis a central bank needs people who can start trading at once, and only a few firms have them. Those same firms own large parts of the markets being rescued. Firms of this size are probably now built into the emergency plans of central banks and finance ministries in several countries, deciding how public money is spent in markets where they hold large positions of their own.

items.title: Large companies given a standing place inside UN agenda-setting
items.claim: Through partnership agreements, the largest companies probably help write part of the UN's agenda on food, health and development, a role that formally belongs to member governments.
items.rule: The UN signed a strategic partnership with the World Economic Forum in 2019, and the first major summit after it, on food systems, grew out of the Forum and was led by the head of an organisation tied to the agrochemical industry.
items.conditions: Partnership discussions are not published; summits are organised by envoys appointed by the Secretary-General rather than negotiated by governments.
items.documented: The June 2019 UN-WEF strategic partnership; the 2021 UN Food Systems Summit and the letters opposing it.
items.would_show: Documents showing a UN outcome text or programme drafted by company representatives through a partnership channel.
items.would_refute: Records of the partnership showing no company role in drafting UN texts or choosing summit leadership.
story: In June 2019 the UN Secretary-General signed a strategic partnership with the World Economic Forum, the Swiss foundation that runs the yearly meeting of business and political leaders in Davos. Its stated aim was to speed up the UN's 2030 development goals through closer coordination between the two. That September more than 400 civil society organisations wrote asking him to end it. They said it gave multinational companies preferential access to the UN and made their executives private advisers to the heads of UN departments.

The first large event after the agreement was the UN Food Systems Summit of 2021. The idea for it came out of the World Economic Forum. The Secretary-General chose as its special envoy the president of the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa, an organisation that promotes fertiliser and commercial seed and has close ties to the agrochemical industry. In February 2020, 176 organisations from 83 countries asked him to withdraw the appointment. By the time the summit opened, more than 500 organisations had signed a call to boycott it, and it went ahead.

What is said inside these partnerships is not published. Part of the agenda the UN sets for food, health and development is probably now drafted with the companies whose products it covers, through partnership channels rather than through the governments that formally run the UN.

items.title: Private donors deciding what the World Health Organization works on
items.claim: A small number of large funders, a private foundation among them, probably decide much of what the World Health Organization actually does, through earmarked money and the staff posts it pays for, without a vote by the member governments that formally run it.
items.rule: About nine-tenths of WHO income is voluntary and almost all of it earmarked; the Gates Foundation is the second-largest funder and its money has gone overwhelmingly to its own chosen diseases; the US has announced it is leaving.
items.conditions: Assessed fees from members are frozen at a small share; donors choose programmes; donor-funded and seconded staff sit inside departments.
items.documented: BMJ Global Health study of Gates Foundation grants to WHO, 2000-2024 (published 2025).
items.would_show: WHO records showing a donor setting the content of WHO guidance or the choice of senior staff through its funding.
items.would_refute: Evidence that WHO priorities set by the World Health Assembly match where earmarked money actually goes.
story: Each member country pays the World Health Organization a set fee based on its wealth and population. Those fees now make up a small part of its income. Around nine-tenths comes from voluntary donations, and almost all of that is earmarked, which means the donor decides which programme the money is spent on.

The second-largest funder after the United States government is the Gates Foundation, a private charity. It gave the WHO 5.5 billion dollars between 2000 and 2024, nearly 10 per cent of the organisation's revenue from 2010 to 2023. Of that, 4.5 billion was earmarked for infectious diseases, 3.2 billion of it for polio, which has long been the WHO's best-funded programme. A study published in BMJ Global Health in 2025 found that the WHO's work follows what its donors choose to pay for, and the foundation's grants have given almost nothing to chronic disease or to building up health systems.
In January 2025 the United States announced that it would leave the WHO, which makes every other large donor more important.

Earmarked money pays for staff and decides which departments grow, and large donors also lend their own staff to the organisation. A few funders probably now decide much of what the world's health agency works on, without the member governments that formally run it ever voting on it.

items.title: Governments using their nationals at the top of UN agencies
items.claim: Several large states probably treat their nationals in senior UN posts as part of their own government, and use them to steer appointments, technical standards and who is allowed to speak.
items.rule: A former head of a UN department described on Chinese state television how he used his post to have a Uyghur activist removed; China led four of the 15 specialised agencies in 2019 and used debt relief and trade pressure in at least one election for those posts.
items.conditions: UN staff swear an oath of independence that is not enforced; agency heads are elected by member states who can be lobbied; technical agencies set standards with little public attention.
items.documented: On the map: the Wu Hongbo case. Reporting on the 2019 FAO election and on China's proposal at the ITU.
items.would_show: A senior UN official shown to have taken instructions from their home government on an agency decision.
items.would_refute: Reviews of agency decisions under the officials concerned finding no pattern favouring their home governments.
story: In 2019 Chinese state television broadcast an interview with Wu Hongbo, who had been the head of the UN's Department of Economic and Social Affairs. He described how he had used that post to have a Uyghur activist removed from a UN forum on indigenous issues, and presented it as defending China's interests.

That year Chinese nationals led four of the UN's 15 specialised agencies. No other country led more than one. In the run-up to the 2019 election for head of the Food and Agriculture Organization, China forgave Cameroon's debt the month before Cameroon withdrew its own candidate, and US officials said China threatened to stop buying key exports from Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay if they did not back its man. He won.

The International Telecommunication Union, which helps set the technical rules for phone and internet networks, was run by a Chinese secretary-general from 2015 to 2022. China used it to put forward a proposal to redesign the internet's underlying architecture in a way critics said would give governments more control over what people can reach.

China is not the only country with many of its people in senior posts. In one count of 378 senior UN positions, Chinese nationals held 14 and Americans 43. UN staff swear to serve the organisation and not their own country, but nothing enforces it. Several large governments probably treat their nationals at the top of UN bodies as their own officials, and use them to influence appointments, standards and who is allowed to speak.

items.title: Owners of the largest technology companies taking roles inside government systems
items.claim: Owners and staff of the largest technology companies are probably taking direct roles inside governments' core systems, with access to data and payments that outside contractors would not normally be given.
items.rule: In 2025 staff of a team set up under the owner of SpaceX and X were given access to the US Treasury's payment system, which a federal judge found had been granted without the usual vetting.
items.conditions: Governments run on software and cloud services from a handful of firms; special government employee status allows people to move in quickly; access logs are not public.
items.documented: Court rulings of February and April 2025 in the Southern District of New York and the District of Columbia.
items.would_show: Evidence that access gained inside a government system was used for the benefit of the companies its holders own or work for.
items.would_refute: Audits by the Treasury inspector general and the GAO finding the access was used only for its stated purpose and no data left the department.
story: On 31 January 2025 the US Treasury gave staff from a new team, the Department of Government Efficiency, access to the system that makes the federal government's payments. In the 2023 financial year that system handled 1.3 billion payments worth 5.4 trillion dollars, including tax refunds, Social Security and federal salaries. It holds the names, Social Security numbers and home addresses of the people being paid. The team had been set up under Elon Musk, whose rocket company, SpaceX, holds large federal contracts.

Many of the team were young engineers brought in as special government employees. Unions and nearly 20 state attorneys general sued. In February a federal judge in New York blocked the access, calling the team's entry into the systems chaotic and haphazard and finding that it had skipped the vetting and training that regular staff go through. A court filing later showed that one staffer had shared sensitive personal information outside the department, against Treasury rules. In April the judge allowed access again once the staff had been trained. The Treasury's inspector general and the Government Accountability Office are auditing it.

Governments everywhere now run on software, data and cloud services supplied by a handful of companies. The owners and staff of those companies are probably taking direct roles inside governments' core systems in more places, with a kind of access to data and payments that an outside contractor would not normally be given.

items.title: Foreign governments paying members of other countries' parliaments
items.claim: Several governments, Russia among them, are probably paying or cultivating sitting lawmakers in other countries' parliaments, choosing those whose positions already suit them, and most of these arrangements have not been found.
items.rule: Belgian and Czech intelligence found in 2024 that Russia had paid members of the European Parliament through a sanctioned news site, and Belgian prosecutors opened a criminal case.
items.conditions: Payments move in cash or through third countries; foreign funding rules for parties and members vary and are weakly enforced; recipients can be paid for speaking rather than voting.
items.documented: Czech sanctions on Voice of Europe and the Belgian investigation (March-April 2024); European Parliament resolution of 25 April 2024.
items.would_show: A court finding or official investigation naming a serving lawmaker paid by a foreign government.
items.would_refute: Investigations of the 2024 allegations finding no payments to serving members.
story: In March 2024 the Czech government put sanctions on Voice of Europe, a news website it said was part of a Russian influence operation. Days later the Belgian prime minister told his parliament that Belgian and Czech intelligence had found that Russia had approached members of the European Parliament and paid some of them to promote its positions. Czech media, citing intelligence officials, said the politicians came from six countries. The payments had been made in cash, outside Belgium. Belgian prosecutors opened a criminal investigation, and the prime minister said Moscow's aim was to get more pro-Russian candidates elected that June and to weaken European support for Ukraine.

The European Parliament passed a resolution on it in April. It also noted that former heads of government and ministers of EU countries, a former German chancellor among them, had taken well-paid posts at Kremlin-controlled energy companies, and that some had stayed on after the full invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Payments like these are rarely found, because they move in cash or through other countries. Several governments, Russia among them, are probably paying or cultivating lawmakers in other countries' parliaments, picking those whose positions already suit them, and most of these arrangements are probably still undiscovered.

items.title: Drug trafficking money reaching presidents and national parties
items.claim: Along the main cocaine routes, trafficking money is probably funding national election campaigns and reaching presidential offices in more countries than have been caught.
items.rule: A Honduran president was convicted in 2024 of protecting traffickers for over a decade while rising to the presidency; he testified that drug money reached virtually all Honduran parties; a national government controls the police, the army and extradition.
items.conditions: Campaign finance is largely unpoliced in transit countries; the main evidence comes from traffickers extradited to the United States.
items.documented: On the map: the conviction of Juan Orlando Hernández (2024).
items.would_show: A court finding that a sitting or former head of government in another transit country was financed by traffickers.
items.would_refute: Campaign finance audits in transit countries finding no trafficking money in national campaigns.
story: Juan Orlando Hernández was president of Honduras from 2014 to 2022. In March 2024 a jury in New York found that he had worked with drug traffickers for more than a decade, taking millions of dollars in bribes as he rose from rural congressman to head of the national congress and then to president, and using the country's police and army to protect their shipments. More than 400 tonnes of cocaine reached the United States under the arrangement. The judge described a 1 million dollar payment from the leader of the Sinaloa cartel, handed to Hernández's brother in 2013. The brother, a former congressman, had already been given a life sentence. Hernández was sentenced to 45 years.

At his trial Hernández denied taking bribes, but said that drug money had been paid to virtually all political parties in Honduras. US court documents have accused leaders of all three of the country's main parties of taking money from traffickers. In December 2025 President Trump pardoned him, saying he had been treated harshly and unfairly, and he was released.

Honduras sits on the route cocaine takes from South America to the United States. A national government controls the police, the army and decisions on extradition. Along this route and others, trafficking money is probably reaching national campaigns and presidents' offices in more countries than have been caught.

items.title: Russian deep-cover officers building careers inside international bodies
items.claim: Russian intelligence officers living under false foreign identities have probably been placed in junior jobs at international courts, UN agencies and European institutions, and some are probably still there.
items.rule: An officer with a twelve-year false identity was accepted for an internship at the International Criminal Court in 2022 and was stopped only at the border. Others trained the same way were found living ordinary lives in Slovenia, Greece and Brazil.
items.conditions: International bodies recruit interns and junior staff from almost every country, largely on paper applications and references. Illegals carry no diplomatic cover and no Russian documents, so the usual checks do not catch them.
items.documented: On the map: the GRU officer who nearly took a job at the ICC (2022).
items.would_show: An official found to have joined an international body under a false identity created by a foreign intelligence service.
items.would_refute: Security reviews of staff at the main international bodies finding no false identities among people hired since 2010.
story: In April 2022 a man travelling as Viktor Muller Ferreira, a 33-year-old Brazilian, landed in the Netherlands to start an internship at the International Criminal Court in The Hague. He had a master's degree from Johns Hopkins University, and one of his professors there had written him a reference. Dutch intelligence stopped him at the airport and sent him back to Brazil. His real name was Sergey Cherkasov. He was an officer of Russian military intelligence, and he had entered Brazil in 2010 using the identity of a Brazilian whose parents had died. The court was investigating Russian war crimes in Ukraine at the time, and the internship would have given him a pass to the building and access to its computer systems.

Russia calls officers like him illegals. They train for years at home, give up contact with their families, and settle abroad as citizens of another country. There they work, pay taxes and raise children, sometimes for more than ten years, before the identity is used for anything. A couple arrested in Slovenia in December 2022 had lived as Argentines in Buenos Aires from 2012 and moved to Ljubljana in 2017. She ran an online art gallery and he ran a small IT company. Their two children spoke Spanish and went to the British international school. In August 2024 the parents were sent to Moscow in a prisoner exchange, and the children were told on the plane that they were Russian.

Within weeks of the Slovenian arrests, two more people suspected of the same work, one living in Greece and one in Brazil, left their homes and disappeared. Dutch intelligence said that illegals are hard to find because they live under an assumed identity and can work for a long time without anyone noticing.

Cherkasov was caught on his way in. Others trained the same way were probably not, and some are likely to be several years into jobs at UN agencies, international courts or European institutions. These bodies take interns and junior staff from almost every country, and the court in The Hague had accepted him on his application and his references. Someone who starts as an intern and stays on can be handling files on Russia within a few years.

items.title: North Korean state workers hired under false names, now spreading to Europe
items.claim: North Korean IT workers using false identities are probably employed at many more companies than have been identified, increasingly in Europe and Asia and at firms that supply defence ministries and governments.
items.rule: US authorities have found them at more than 100 companies in one set of cases alone, Google reports them moving into Europe and applying to defence and government employers, and North Korea is said to have sent thousands of such workers abroad.
items.conditions: Remote hiring rarely involves meeting the worker; laptops can be operated from abroad through intermediaries; enforcement has been concentrated in the United States.
items.documented: On the map: the Arizona and New Jersey laptop-farm cases.
items.would_show: A European or Asian employer, especially a defence supplier or government body, found to have employed a North Korean worker under a false identity.
items.would_refute: Systematic checks by European employers and agencies finding no such workers outside the cases already charged.
story: A company advertises a remote job for a software developer. The person who gets it is using a stolen American identity. The company posts the work laptop to an address in the United States, where a paid helper plugs it in alongside others, and the worker logs into it from abroad. The salary ends up with the North Korean government.

In June 2025 the US Justice Department announced searches of 29 of these laptop farms in 16 states. The workers involved had used more than 80 stolen identities to get jobs at more than 100 American companies. US agencies had warned in 2022 that North Korea had sent thousands of IT workers overseas.

Google's threat intelligence group reported in April 2025 that the workers were moving into Europe as American employers became more careful. One of them had run at least 12 false identities across Europe and the United States, and had applied for jobs at defence companies and government bodies. People who help them get identity documents and receive their pay have been found in Britain and elsewhere in Europe. Since late 2024 some of the workers have threatened to publish company data unless they are paid.

Most of the charges so far have been brought in the United States, where the FBI has been looking for these workers since 2022. Many more are probably on payrolls in Europe and Asia, including at contractors working for defence ministries, and some have probably been asked to collect information as well as earn wages.

items.title: Governments with their own people on the staff of social media companies
items.claim: Some governments have probably placed or recruited their own people among the employees of social media companies who can see users' private data, particularly in the local offices those governments now require the companies to open.
items.rule: Saudi Arabia did this at Twitter and the employee was convicted; a whistleblower said Twitter's executives believed India had done the same; India, Russia and Turkey now require platforms to keep staff in the country.
items.conditions: Local staff with access to account data are within reach of local police and courts; insider access at platforms has been poorly logged; transparency reports count formal requests only.
items.documented: On the map: Saudi officials paying Twitter staff to look up critics' accounts, and the conviction of Ahmad Abouammo (2022).
items.would_show: An employee of a platform shown to have been placed or recruited by a government and to have passed it user data outside legal process.
items.would_refute: Independent audits of insider access at the main platforms' local offices finding no unexplained look-ups of accounts the host government was pursuing.
story: Between 2013 and 2015 a media partnerships manager on Twitter's Middle East team looked up the private details of anonymous accounts that criticised the Saudi government, including email addresses and phone numbers, and passed them to an adviser to the Saudi crown prince. He was paid at least 300,000 dollars and given a luxury watch. A Twitter engineer accused of the same thing left for Saudi Arabia before he could be charged. The manager, Ahmad Abouammo, was convicted in San Francisco in August 2022 and sentenced to three and a half years.

Later that month a whistleblower complaint by Twitter's former head of security became public. It said the company's executives believed the Indian government had succeeded in placing agents on Twitter's payroll, with unsupervised access to user data, during a period of large protests in India. Twitter disputed his account. He said supporting material had been given to the national security division of the US Justice Department and to the Senate intelligence committee. No finding on the claim has been published.

Several governments now require large platforms to employ staff inside their borders. India's 2021 rules make them appoint a compliance officer, a contact for the police and a grievance officer, all living in India, and the compliance officer can be held personally liable. Russia has required foreign platforms with more than 500,000 daily users to open a local office since 2022, and Turkey passed a similar law in 2020.

These rules put employees who can reach account data within reach of the government that wants it. In some of these countries the security services have probably gone further and placed or recruited their own people in the local offices, as Saudi Arabia did at Twitter's headquarters.

items.title: Foreign spies posing as recruiters to sign up officials
items.claim: Some of the many officials approached by foreign intelligence services posing as recruiters and consultancies have probably accepted paid work and are still in post, passing on information without having been identified.
items.rule: One such fake consultancy drew more than 400 CVs, nine in ten from cleared US personnel, and paid some of them for reports; MI5 counts tens of thousands of such approaches in Britain alone.
items.conditions: The first contact looks like ordinary freelance or job-market activity; paid reports are small and easy to hide; few cases reach court.
items.documented: The 2020 guilty plea in Washington of a Singaporean who ran a fake consultancy for Chinese intelligence; on the map, fake research jobs used to recruit Philippine defence staff.
items.would_show: A serving official found to have been recruited through a fake recruiter or consultancy and to have supplied information while in post.
items.would_refute: Follow-up of the approaches reported to security services finding that none led to paid work by serving officials.
story: In 2018 a Singaporean researcher living in Washington was told by his contacts in Chinese intelligence to set up a consulting company and post job advertisements online. He gave the company the same name as a well-known American public affairs firm. More than 400 people sent him their CVs, and nine in ten came from US military and government staff with security clearances. He passed the most useful ones to his handlers.

He then paid some of the people he found to write reports, telling them the reports were for clients in Asia. One worked on the F-35 fighter jet programme and had told him he was short of money. Another was an army officer, who was paid through his wife's bank account. The Singaporean pleaded guilty in July 2020.

Britain's security service, MI5, said in 2021 that at least 10,000 people in Britain had been approached on LinkedIn over five years by fake profiles linked to hostile states. In October 2023 its director general put the number of online approaches by suspected Chinese agents at more than 20,000. The first message usually offers a job or paid consulting work.

Very few of these approaches have ended in a prosecution. Some of the people who agreed to write a paid report are probably still in government or military jobs and still in contact with the same 'consultancy'. Each early step looks like ordinary freelance work, so it is unlikely to be reported.

items.title: Staff in legislatures whose salaries are paid by outside interests
items.claim: On new technical subjects such as artificial intelligence, a share of the staff helping legislators write the rules are probably paid, directly or through nonprofits, by the industries and funders the rules will affect.
items.rule: In 2023 a tech-funded foundation was paying more than a dozen AI fellows in Senate offices and federal departments, and a second programme placed AI staff partly paid by five of the largest tech companies; outside-funded fellows number in the hundreds across the US government.
items.conditions: Legislative offices have few staff with technical expertise; fellowships are free to the office; funding can pass through nonprofits that hide its source.
items.documented: Politico's reporting of October and December 2023 on AI fellows in Congress.
items.would_show: A fellow shown to have drafted legislative text or briefed a member on the instruction of, or in coordination with, the body that paid the fellow's salary.
items.would_refute: Published records of fellows' funders and work showing no drafting or briefing on matters affecting those funders.
story: In October 2023 Politico reported that a foundation funded mainly by a tech billionaire was paying the salaries of more than a dozen artificial intelligence fellows. They were working in US Senate offices, on the House science committee, and at the departments of Defense, Homeland Security and State. The foundation had set aside nearly 3 million dollars in 2022 for the first group. The salaries were paid through a nonprofit it had effectively set up that year, which a former official of the Office of Congressional Ethics said looked like an attempt to hide the programme's ties to the funder. The foundation had connections to leading AI companies, and the fellows were working on the rules that would apply to those companies.

In December 2023 Politico reported a second programme that had placed six AI staff in Senate offices, with salaries partly paid by five of the largest technology companies. Outside-funded fellows work in the hundreds across the US government. One programme alone had sent nearly 100 technology fellows to congressional offices since 2015.

A fellow can draft questions for hearings, brief the member and write parts of a bill. Few legislative offices anywhere have staff who understand subjects like AI, and a fellow comes free. On subjects like this, a share of the people helping to write the rules in several legislatures are probably paid by the companies and funders those rules will cover.

items.title: Gangs owning investment funds and payment companies
items.claim: Large criminal groups probably own or control licensed financial firms, especially small payment companies and investment funds, in several countries, using them to hold and move money without relying on corrupt staff at a bank.
items.rule: Brazilian authorities allege that the PCC held money in at least 40 investment funds and moved it through payment companies acting as parallel banks; smaller financial firms are cheaper to set up and less closely supervised than banks.
items.conditions: Pooled accounts hide the end customer from the bank; fund administrators and payment firms face lighter reporting rules in many countries; the firms look like ordinary businesses.
items.documented: On the map: the PCC's money placed in São Paulo funds, fintechs and fuel firms, and its control of more than a thousand petrol stations (investigation, 2025-26).
items.would_show: A licensed financial firm outside Brazil shown by regulators or a court to be owned or controlled by a criminal group.
items.would_refute: Beneficial-ownership checks of payment firms and fund vehicles in the highest-risk countries finding no criminal ownership.
story: On 28 August 2025 Brazilian police, prosecutors and tax officials carried out searches in several states, including at 42 addresses on Avenida Faria Lima in São Paulo, the centre of the country's financial industry. They were investigating the Primeiro Comando da Capital, or PCC, a gang that began in São Paulo's prisons in the 1990s.

According to the federal tax authority, about 1,000 petrol stations linked to the group moved 52 billion reais, roughly 9.5 billion US dollars, between 2020 and 2024, while paying far less tax than that turnover required. The authorities say the money was kept in at least 40 investment funds holding about 30 billion reais, run by firms in the financial district, and moved through payment companies that they described as working like parallel banks.

Many of these payment companies held their customers' money in a single pooled account at a bank. The bank could see one account belonging to the payment company, and not the people whose money was in it. After the searches the tax authority said payment companies would be brought under the same reporting rules as banks.

In this case the gang did not need a corrupt bank employee, because it appears to have controlled the funds and payment firms itself. Large criminal groups in other countries are probably doing the same, since a small payment company or a fund is cheaper to set up than a bank and in many countries is supervised less closely.

items.title: Gangs placing their own people in police stations and welfare offices
items.claim: Criminal networks in Sweden, and probably in other countries with large gang economies, are likely putting forward their own members and relatives for jobs in the police, social services and prisons, not only corrupting staff who are already employed.
items.rule: Swedish police have recorded hundreds of suspected leaks to criminals, several through employees with family or romantic ties to gang members, and Swedish state bodies report that groups target municipal staff and that agencies' defences against infiltration are not effective.
items.conditions: Most municipal and many agency jobs carry no security vetting; staff turnover is high; follow-up checks after hiring are weak, as the national audit office found in 2026.
items.documented: Dagens Nyheter's April 2024 reporting on police leaks; Brå report 2025:4 on influence over municipal staff; the Swedish National Audit Office's February 2026 audit.
items.would_show: A public employee shown by an investigation or court to have been recruited into the job on a criminal group's instruction and to have acted for it there.
items.would_refute: Reviews of the leak cases finding that every employee involved was drawn in after hiring, with none placed by a group.
story: In April 2024 the Swedish newspaper Dagens Nyheter reported that the police had recorded more than 500 suspected leaks of information from inside the force to criminals since 2018. At least 30 police employees had been judged security risks and had resigned or been made to leave. Some of them were dating gang members or were related to them, and had passed on information from police systems.

Sweden's own state bodies have since described the same problem in other parts of government. The national crime prevention council, Brå, reported in 2025 that criminal and extremist groups try to influence municipal staff, especially in social services, where employees make decisions about benefits, housing support and children's care. It found that local staff are less protected than members of parliament or central government officials. In February 2026 the national audit office examined three agencies, among them the prison and probation service, and concluded that their work against infiltration was not effective. Checks on staff after they were hired were falling short, and many prison staff were unsure how to report a suspicion.

Most of the employees found so far were drawn in after they already had the job, through a partner or a family member. Gangs are probably also putting their own people forward for these jobs: a member's girlfriend or cousin applying to the police, or someone close to the group taking work as a benefits officer or a care worker. This is likely to be happening wherever gangs have grown large enough to need a regular flow of information and public money from inside the state, not only in Sweden.

items.title: Cartels deciding who becomes mayor
items.claim: In parts of Mexico and other countries with powerful drug-trafficking groups, those groups are probably choosing or paying for many local candidates before campaigns begin, so that a share of mayors already work for them on the day they take office.
items.rule: Violence against candidates is concentrated at the municipal level, where the police and local contracts are controlled, and an electoral court has already annulled one mayoral election because organised crime had removed the competition.
items.conditions: Thousands of municipal offices are contested at once; mayors control municipal police, permits and public works; candidates who are threatened usually withdraw quietly.
items.documented: Data Cívica's count of 34 candidates murdered in the 2023-24 cycle; the annulled 2021 election in Jilotlán de los Dolores, Jalisco.
items.would_show: A mayor shown in court records or an official investigation to have been selected or financed by a criminal group before the election and to have acted for it in office.
items.would_refute: Audits of municipal campaigns in the highest-risk states finding no criminal money and no candidates withdrawn under pressure beyond those already recorded.
story: Mexico's election of 2 June 2024 filled more than 20,000 posts. Between September 2023 and polling day the research group Data Cívica counted 34 candidates and would-be candidates murdered and 95 more attacked. In the previous national election, in 2021, 85 per cent of the murdered candidates had been running for a municipal office rather than a state or federal one.

A Mexican mayor controls the municipal police, local permits and the town's spending on roads and buildings. Researchers who follow the violence say this is why it falls so heavily on local races, and why deals between officials and organised crime are most common at that level.

In 2021, in Jilotlán de los Dolores, a municipality in the state of Jalisco, two of the three candidates for mayor withdrew after threats from local gangs. The third won unopposed. A federal electoral court then annulled the result, ruling that organised crime had made a free election there impossible.

Murders and withdrawals are recorded. Candidates who are picked or financed by a criminal group before campaigning begins are not, and there are probably many more of them, since a candidate the group already controls is never threatened. Data Cívica has also found that each attack on a candidate lowers turnout in that place by 1.3 per cent, and by 3 per cent when the person attacked already holds office.
